cues: Why speed matters in a truck.
FMCSA reports that 11,775 lives were lost in crashes involving speed in 2023, roughly one-third of all traffic fatalities on U.S. roads.
Speed makes every crash worse.
Crash energy grows with the square of speed: if you double your speed, you carry about four times the energy into a crash.
Speed also takes away time.
At 65 miles per hour a truck covers about 95 feet every second, so you have less time to see a hazard, decide and act.
For you, speeding can mean injury or death, convictions on your driving record, CDL disqualification and loss of your ability to work as a professional driver.
Scenario: You are a little behind on a 300-mile run with a 65 mile-per-hour limit.
Driving 70 instead of 65 would save only about 20 minutes over the whole trip, and it would be illegal and raise your crash risk the entire way.
Key takeaway: Small speed increases save very little time but add a lot of risk and crash energy.
Posted limits, restrictions and the law.
Under 49 CFR 392.2, every commercial motor vehicle must be operated according to the laws of the jurisdiction it is in.
That includes posted and regulated speed limits.
Speed limits are set by states and local authorities.
Some states post lower limits for trucks than for cars, and limits drop in towns, school zones and work zones.
The truck limit is the one that applies to you.
Under 49 CFR 383.51, Table 2, speeding excessively, meaning 15 miles per hour or more above the regulated or posted limit, is a serious traffic violation.
A second serious traffic violation conviction in a separate incident within 3 years while driving a CMV means a 60-day disqualification from driving a CMV.
A third means 120 days.
Convictions in your personal vehicle can also count if they lead to a license suspension or revocation.
Following too closely and improper or erratic lane changes, which often come with speeding, are also serious traffic violations under the same table.
Under 49 CFR 392.6, a motor carrier must not schedule a run, or permit or require driving, in a time that would need speeds above the posted limits.
Scenario: A driver gets two speeding tickets for 16 miles per hour over the limit in a CMV, two years apart, and is convicted of both.
Under 49 CFR 383.51 the driver faces a 60-day CDL disqualification.
Key takeaway: 15 or more over is a serious violation.
Two serious violations in 3 years means 60 days off the road.
Adjust speed for road, traffic and weather.
Under 49 CFR 392.14, extreme caution is required when snow, ice, sleet, fog, mist, rain, dust or smoke affect visibility or traction.
Speed must be reduced.
If conditions become dangerous enough, stop driving until the truck can be operated safely.
The posted limit is a maximum for ideal conditions, not a target.
Common CDL guidance: on a wet road, slow down by about one-third.
On packed snow, slow down by about half or more.
On ice, slow to a crawl and get off the road as soon as it is safe.
At night, in fog or in heavy rain, drive at a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see ahead.
Keep a safe following distance: at least one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length, plus one more second above 40 miles per hour.
For a 70-foot rig at highway speed that is about 8 seconds.
Add more in bad weather.
Do not use cruise control on wet, icy or snowy roads.
Scenario: Heavy rain starts on a 65 mile-per-hour highway.
Slowing by about one-third means about 43 miles per hour or lower, with cruise control off and extra following distance.
Key takeaway: Legal is not always safe.
Federal rules require you to slow down when weather or visibility gets worse.
Stopping distance and reaction time.
FMCSA: large trucks traveling at highway speeds can need the length of up to two football fields to stop, and stopping distance increases with heavier loads or poor road conditions.

Total stopping distance has four parts: perception distance while you notice the hazard, reaction distance while you move to the brake, brake lag while the air brakes build pressure, and braking distance until the truck stops.
Braking distance grows with the square of speed.
Going from 50 to 70 miles per hour roughly doubles your braking distance.
Every second you spend noticing and reacting at 65 miles per hour is about 95 feet traveled before the brakes even start working.
FMCSA advises scanning about 15 seconds ahead, about a quarter mile on interstates, and checking mirrors every 8 to 10 seconds.
Scenario: Traffic is stopped just over a hill crest.
At 65 miles per hour your truck may need close to two football fields to stop, so you must already be at a speed that lets you stop within the road you can see.
Key takeaway: Lower speed gives you more time to react and much less distance to stop.
Work zones.
FMCSA warns that work zones bring lane shifts, sudden stops, uneven road surfaces and moving workers and equipment, and that fatal work zone crashes continue to rise.
A posted work zone speed limit is a legal limit.
Many states increase fines for violations in work zones, and the rules vary by state.
Speeding 15 or more over in a work zone is still a serious violation under 49 CFR 383.51.
FMCSA guidance: slow down, keep extra following space and be prepared to stop.
Obey all work zone signs and signals, scan ahead for changing traffic patterns, and watch for road workers and flag crews.
Scenario: You see Road Work Ahead, Speed Limit 45.
Traffic around you is still doing 60.
Slow to 45 or less, increase your following distance and watch for lane shifts and workers, even if other drivers do not slow down.
Key takeaway: In a work zone the posted limit applies to you no matter what traffic is doing.
Curves, ramps, downgrades and crash prevention.
FMCSA notes that speeds on curve warning signs are often set for passenger vehicles, so trucks should slow down even further.
A loaded trailer has a high center of gravity and can roll over below the posted advisory speed.
Slow down before you enter a curve or ramp and finish braking on the straight, not in the curve.
Large vehicles may gain speed quickly downhill.
Choose a lower gear before you start down, and do not ride the brakes, because they can overheat and fade.
Check your speedometer after every speed limit sign, on every downgrade and when the highway enters a town, where limits can drop quickly.
Scenario: An off-ramp has a 35 mile-per-hour advisory and you are loaded.
Slow to below the advisory speed before the ramp curve begins, and do your braking on the straight.
Key takeaway: Slow down before the curve, pick the gear before the hill, and watch your speed where limits change.
Delivery pressure and driver responsibility.
Schedule pressure never makes speeding legal.
Under 49 CFR 392.6 a carrier must not schedule runs that require speeding, and under 49 CFR 392.2 you must obey speed limits.
If you will be late, notify dispatch as soon as you can do so safely and legally, and keep driving at a safe, legal speed.
Dispatch handles the appointment with the customer.
This policy wording is proposed and must be confirmed by management.
Do not text or hold a phone while driving to update dispatch.
Texting and hand-held phone violations are also serious traffic violations under 49 CFR 383.51.
Plan realistic trip times that allow for traffic, weather and required breaks.
Never try to make up time by speeding.
Scenario: You are running 30 minutes late and the receiver may cancel the appointment.
Notify dispatch when it is safe to do so and continue at a safe, legal speed.
A lost appointment can be rebooked; a crash cannot be undone.
Key takeaway: You control the speed of your truck.
No schedule is worth a crash or your CDL.
Summary: key takeaways.
Key takeaway: Speed increases crash energy with the square of speed and leaves less time to react.
Key takeaway: Speeding 15 or more over the limit is a serious violation.
Two convictions in 3 years means a 60-day CDL disqualification.
Key takeaway: Federal rules require you to slow down in hazardous conditions, and the posted limit is a maximum, not a target.
Key takeaway: Trucks can need up to two football fields to stop.
Slow down before curves, ramps, downgrades and work zones.
Key takeaway: If you are running late, notify dispatch when safe and keep a safe, legal speed.
